theme: Edom falls, God defends his people
readingInstruction: Read Obadiah (one chapter, 21 verses). This is the shortest book in the Old Testament. It is a prophecy against Edom, Israel’s brother nation, for the pride and violence shown to Judah. Read it in one sitting.
settingTheScene: Edom descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin brother. The two nations had a history of rivalry. When Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, Edom stood by, gloated, and even took part, looting and handing over fugitives. Obadiah’s prophecy was likely given soon after. Psalm 137:7 and Lamentations 4:21 also remember Edom’s betrayal. The book answers a question: will God let this stand?
observation: “The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock” (v. 3).
“Though you soar aloft like the eagle… from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD” (v. 4).
“Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you” (v. 10).
“On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth” (v. 11).
“You should not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune” (v. 12).
“You should not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity” (v. 13).
“For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15).
“And the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).
interpretation:
Edom’s capital Sela, “the rock,” was built in the cliffs of the mountains, in a nearly impregnable position. The Edomites thought they were safe: “Who will bring me down to the ground?” Obadiah says God will. Pride has deceived them. No place is high enough to escape God’s reach.

The chief charge is against Edom’s treatment of Judah. Verses 10 to 14 lay out a series of failures, each introduced by “you should not.” Edom stood aloof when strangers invaded. It gloated, rejoiced, boasted, entered the gate, looted, and cut off the fugitives. This is not a case of ordinary rivalry. It is a betrayal of kin. And that is what makes it worse. A brother stands by while his brother is attacked.

Notice what is condemned: standing aloof counts as a sin. “On the day that you stood aloof… you were like one of them.” Passive indifference is complicity. Gloating over the misfortune of someone else is a serious sin. Proverbs 24:17-18 says, “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls.”

God’s judgment is described by the principle of reciprocity: “As you have done, it shall be done to you.” The proud will be brought low.

But the book does not end in judgment alone. It ends with a vision of deliverance: “On Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy.” Jacob will possess his own. “Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.” This final sentence is the aim of the whole prophecy: God’s kingdom will prevail, and all pride will fall before it.

Obadiah is a reminder that God sees how we treat others, especially when they fall.
connection: Matthew 25:41-45 says that what we do or fail to do for the least of these, we do or fail to do for Christ. Luke 10:30-37 shows the priest and Levite who passed by on the other side. Proverbs 24:17: “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls.” James 4:6: God opposes the proud. Revelation 11:15: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.” 1 Corinthians 12:26: if one member suffers, all suffer together.
application:
Think of a person whose downfall you secretly enjoyed. Confess it, and pray for them.

Ask whether you have “stood aloof” when someone in your family, church, or community was in trouble.

Be on guard against the pride of security, the sense that nothing can touch you.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to humble the pride of your heart.
Ask him to keep you from gloating over another’s misfortune.
Ask him to give you a heart that grieves with those who grieve.
